newsitem.title: INDIA: Commodities-India's strides seen far short of goal.
newsitem.headline: Commodities-India's strides seen far short of goal.

text.p: India has made giant strides in agriculture during 50 years of independence but production shortfalls in key commodities continue to dog the country, sector analysts said on Sunday.
Echoing the government's concern at stagnating food output in the face of rising population, Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujaral on Saturday called for steps to boost productivity.
"There are some reasons to be satisfied about it (agriculture), but there are many reasons not to be satisfied about it," he told a meeting of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).

"I think productivity is now causing anxiety....I see the ominous signs (of productivity), I hate, I hesitate to use the word, coming towards a halt. And if that halt comes, we'll be in difficulty," he said.
Official figures show that India's foodgrains production had more than trebled to 198.20 million tonnes by 1996/97, ended March, from 54.92 million in 1949/50.
But India's population in the same period had risen to 960 million from around 320 million.
"India has achieved a lot. But we have a long way to go," said G.R Saini, a former economist with the Indian government and the Rome-based Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
"Food production must outpace population growth, if India has to bridge the gap between demand and supply," Saini said.

India imported foodgrains in the initial years after independence from British rule in 1947. But a "Green Revolution" achieved in the 1960s through high-yield varieties boosted the country's foodgrains output.
India's sugarcane production rose to 271 million tonnes by 1996/97 from 135 million in 1969/70.
In plantation crops of coffee, tea, spices and natural rubber too India has made enough progress. It is surplus in coffee, tea and spices and self-sufficient in rubber.
Analysts said India's agricultural growth, however, had been punctuated with lapses and inconsistency.
"The green revolution should not have ended as a one-time phenomenon. A periodic thrust needs to be given to agriculture to step up production on a continous basis," Saini said.
India set up a technology mission for oilseeds in mid-1980s and their production doubled to 22 million by 1993/94 but has since stagnated.

The country became the world's largest importer of edible oils in 1987/88, buying up to 1.9 million tonnes due to poor oilseeds production. Its imports had fallen to 300,000 tonnes by the early 1990's before rising again to 1.2 million in 1996/97.
On the plus side, India exported five million tonnes of rice and two million tonnes of wheat in 1995/96. The very next year it imported more than two million tonnes of wheat.
India has also boosted the production of soybean, a relatively new oilseed, to four million tonnes in the last two decades.
The country has been lucky to enjoy good monsoon rains for the last 10 years in a row, after a serious drought in 1986/87.
"But one monsoon can make all the difference. Its failure in one year can create severe production shortfalls, push up prices and trigger imports," said G.C. Iyer, a commodities analyst.
"In the last 50 years we have not done what we should have, especially in the field of water management," Iyer said.

"India has all the factors essential for agriculture - land, sunshine, rainfall, necessary climate and labour," he said. "But what is lacking is management to bring all these factors together and exploit them."
Iyer said the most criucial of these was water management which had been neglected. India had woken up to dry farming only recently, he added.
Gujral's speech at the CII meeting too stressed the need for dry farming.
"Our research and development must aim towards dry farming," Gujral said. "As water problem continues, we have to think of new technologies."
Analysts said India should step up its foodgrains production to at least 225 million tonnes in the next decade to meet its growing needs.
"It's big challenge that can make managers of agriculture in India rather uncomfortable," Iyer said.
